newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia details 3-yr extended arrangement with IMF.
newsitem.headline: Croatia details 3-yr extended arrangement with IMF.

text.p: Croatia hopes a new $486 million loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would help it press on with key structural reforms in the next three years, central bank and government officials said on Friday.

To secure further IMF aid under a so-called extended fund facility (EFF), Croatia had to adopt a variety of medium-term policies in the monetary and fiscal sphere. They were approved by the Fund as a base for the new loan.
"This is our programme and we would be implementing it even without the IMF('s loan)," Deputy Prime Minister Borislav Skegro told a news conference.
But he said significance of the new arrangement was great, and not only in terms of financing but because it would help the country's image in the international financial circles.
The EFF comes at a time when the government has to tackle tough problems such as company restructuring and bank rehabilitation.
It must develop fledgling financial markets and set up a proper infrastructure, introduce a new payments system and also complete privatisation of the economy.
The EFF represents a continuation of an 18-month stand-by loan in support of its basic stabilisation efforts which expired in spring last year.
The fund's financial backing is designed to help Croatia create conditions for a healthy economic growth, basically by maintaining a stable macroeconomic environment.
It will be used to boost to the National Bank of Croatia's international reserves, now representing some 3-1/2 months worth of imports.
Croatia has been an IMF member since December 1992. The country's quota, determining its voting rights and access to IMF financing, is 261.6 million SDRs (about $360 million).
Total amount of aid through 1999 was put by government officials at 353.16 million special drawing rights (SDRs).
The funds will be withdrawn in quarterly lots and Croatia expects to use some $158 million of the total in the first year, said the central bank governor Marko Skreb.
He described terms of the loan, as "very favourable":
"We have a 4-1/2 year grace period and 10-year repayment, with the interest rate of around 4.2 percent."
The government took upon itself to keep inflation at a low 3-4 percent and preserve a stable rate of the national currency, the kuna, Skreb said.
It will also have to limit the central budget deficit to under 3.0 percent and reduce the current account deficit, seen at some six percent of the gross domestic product this year.
The fund aid was linked to a World Bank loan for enterprise and financial structuring which is expected to be approved in May, Skreb added.
